description.en: Palace courtyards, museum halls and the slow lanes of Seochon and Samcheong-dong.
A dense grid of shops, street food and the oldest market in the city.
Curved architecture, fabric markets and the printing alleys of Euljiro.
Converted factories, a long green park and the city’s busiest café street.
Music venues, student streets and a converted railway park.
The national museum, a war memorial, and the most international street in Seoul.
Riverside parks, a department store and the city’s financial district.
Underground malls, an observation tower and a large Olympic park.

note.en: Where you buy the entry ticket. The same word appears at towers and terminals.
무료 next to it means free entry.
관람 is viewing. You will see it at museums too.
관 at the end means a public hall or building.
기획 전시 is a special exhibition.
Leave your bag before going in.
A cheap, filling market meal. The word is on dozens of stalls.
Steamed or fried, sold by the plate.
A hand-cut noodle soup, common in market alleys.
The most common street food sign in the country.
Often sold at the same stall as 떡볶이.
A loanword — read it aloud and you will hear it.
Another loanword you can decode on sight.
Also used at restaurants for food to go.
The plain, general word for an eating place.
Cheap, quick Korean snacks — kimbap, ramyeon, fried bites.
From the German Hof. Usually paired with 치킨 on the same sign.
점 at the end means shop.
면세 means tax exempt.
세일 is also used on the same signs.
대여 means rental. Wearing hanbok gets you free palace entry.
A small studio where things are made and sold.
집 at the end means house or shop.
The board showing where everything is. 도 means map or drawing.
A Konglish loanword — marks the spot with the best view.
The reason you queued for the lift.
기념 means commemoration.
Machines that reload T-money cards.
Ask here for route help or lost items.
로 at the end means road or path.
Benches and shade. 쉼 means rest.
Usually with a green cross outside.
치과 is dental, 내과 is internal medicine.
ATMs are labelled ATM or 현금인출기.
Useful near markets and tourist streets.
The word itself. Everything else on a restroom door is a variation of this.
남자 means man. Often shown with a blue plate or figure.
여자 means woman. Often shown with a red plate or figure.
Marked separately in stations, museums and larger cafés.
Common in department stores and large stations.
On the door you are about to walk into. Push, don’t pull.
The other half of every Korean door.
입 is enter, 구 is opening. The pair shows up on buildings and stations.
Subway exits are numbered: 3번 출구 is Exit 3.
Always on the green running-figure sign.
Hung on the door while the shop is serving.
The shop exists and is staffed — it just isn’t serving you yet.
금일 휴무 means closed today.
Convenience stores, saunas and some cafés.
금 is to forbid. You will see it on 금지 signs too.
Museums, some shops, and parts of palaces.
Staff-only doors and closed-off areas.
주의 means caution. It pairs with many other words.
Low doorways in older buildings and markets.
지하 is underground, 철 is rail.
정류장 is the stop itself.
On subway platforms where lines meet.
Follow it to reach the train.
Paired with 엘리베이터 and 에스컬레이터 on station signs.
A loanword — read it aloud and you will hear it.
편의 means convenience, 점 means shop.
Often labelled ATM as well.
무료 와이파이 means free Wi-Fi.
In stations, malls and museums.
Red and white branding across the country.
Free to use. Parks, stations and tourist streets point to the nearest one.
On restroom and fitting-room doors. 중 means in the middle of.
In many restrooms the sign asks you to put paper in the bin, not the toilet.
Found in both men’s and women’s restrooms in newer buildings.
Most Korean toilets have one. The buttons are labelled in Korean too.
Smoking is only allowed in these rooms or marked zones.
In shops, gyms and swimming pools. 실 at the end means room.
Free drinking water in parks and public buildings.
One restroom shared by men and women, common in small cafés.
By lifts, entrances and counters.
Wait for it to open. 문 means door.
On lift buttons, next to 닫힘.
The other lift button. Press 열림 if someone is still coming.
The front entrance of a palace, school or park.
Often closer to the subway than the main gate.
On some stairs and corridors. 좌 is left.
The usual rule in stations. 우 is right.
On arrows in stations and malls.
The usual way is blocked. Follow the arrow around.
Hotels and department stores. A side door is usually next to it.
비상 means emergency, the same word as in 비상구.
On lift buttons and stairwell signs. Some rooftops are cafés or gardens.
층 means floor. Lifts show it as B1.
On doors that let the heating or cooling out.
A desk or board where you can ask the way.
Followed by the times, for example 11:00~21:00.
Many restaurants close between lunch and dinner, often 15:00~17:00.
매주 월요일 정기 휴무 means closed every Monday.

meaning.en: Open every day of the year

note.en: No day off at all.
A loanword used on new shops, often with a date: 10월 오픈.
입장 마감 means last admission.
The kitchen stops taking orders after this time.
Banks, post offices and clinics may pause service.
On ticket windows and food stalls.
The shop is closed for a while, not for good.
Opposite of 주말 (weekend). Hours often differ between them.
Usually on a red or yellow sign. Stay back.
금지 again — anything followed by it is forbidden.
반입 means bringing in. Common at museums and theatres.
On exhibits and shop displays.
발밑 is under your feet. Gaps, steps and uneven floors.
Expect detours or closed exits.
반려동물 is a companion animal.
Red cabinets in stations and corridors.
On lifts, ticket machines and vending machines.
A stronger form of no fire, near fuel or gas.
A loanword. Stand still or walk carefully.
타는 곳 means where you board.
The subway screen shows which side the doors will open.
For older people, pregnant women and people with disabilities.
Pink seats on Seoul subways. Leave them empty.
차 means vehicle.
Check it before a late night out.
Stops at fewer stations. Some lines run both.
Everyone gets off here.
시청 방면 means toward City Hall. Pick the platform by it.
Painted stripes on the road.
장 at the end means place.
On airport railroad and bus signs.
Bus card readers at the back door say 하차. Tap again when you get off.
무 means without. 무료 입장 is free entry.
Water, side dishes or returning trays are up to you.
Where you pay. 계산 means paying the bill.
Machines ask if you want one printed.
Charging stations in cafés, stations and malls.
Coin-operated, often open 24 hours.
You will see one on almost every block.
Smaller local posts are called 파출소 or 지구대.
Maps and help in English. Look for the i sign.
Bins are split by type: 일반 (general), 플라스틱, 캔, 종이.
